The bill for troubleshooting missing feature flags in a healthtech tenant experiment includes key lookups, scheduled comparison runs, captured errors, and retained evidence. Safe fallback defaults keep the established workflow active while that investigation proceeds. For a storage design, retained evidence deserves an explicit calculation before anyone proposes keeping every response indefinitely. In an illustrative workload—not a measured deployment—100 tenant cohorts producing one 2 KB summary per day generate 200 KB daily; retaining 30 days requires 6 MB before indexes, replication, and encoding overhead. Keeping 20 KB instead makes that 60 MB. Payload size changes this term tenfold; a different flag service doesn't erase it.

articles.author: hammi
articles.description:
i'm the dev behind RKMovies, a 1.17 mb native 4k player for android, with a 29.5 mb windows build on the side. one constraint i gave myself early: subtitles must not burn in amoled screens, and total playback ram has to stay under 15 mb on 2 gb phones. this is how the subtitle engine actually works.
the obvious implementation is a div stacked over the video that you re-render on every cue. two problems with that. on amoled, every static pixel is a burn-in timer, and subtitle blocks sit still for seconds at the bottom of the frame. and re-creating dom nodes per cue on a budget phone is gc churn you feel as jank during seeks.
so the player renders webvtt cues onto a single canvas layered above the video surface. the parser keeps a sorted cue list plus a sliding window of the 3 active cues, and the canvas only repaints when that active set changes or when you seek. text metrics are measured once per style run and cached, so a two hour movie does not re-measure the same words thousands of times.
one canvas layer costs one extra composite pass on the gpu. the mediacodec hw decode path underneath is untouched, which is why the ram number holds under 15 mb during 4k hevc playback.
upstream sources hand out srt, players want webvtt, so the app converts in memory at load: drop the index line, swap comma decimals for dot timestamps, re-wrap overlong lines. it's a small state machine and it keeps the bundled parser tiny, which matters when your whole apk is 1.17 mb.
grab the android build on the apk download page, or the windows one on the pc edition page. the home page is here if you want the full feature list.
articles.title: how my 1.17 mb player renders webvtt subtitles on a canvas (no amoled burn-in, no dom churn)

Our book review site needed a feature readers would actually use, and that other sites would want to link to. We settled on a reading speed test, then found that most existing tests share a flaw: skim the passage, press stop, and you're suddenly reading at 1,000 words per minute.
Here's how we built one that pushes back, in a single React client component inside a Next.js app.
The component is a small state machine with four stages: intro → reading → quiz → result.
const [stage, setStage] = useState<"intro" | "reading" | "quiz" | "result">("intro");

We wrote three original passages (about 300 words each), each with three multiple-choice questions. Original text matters: nobody has read it before, and there's no copyright question.
Date.now() can jump if the system clock changes, so we tim…

TL;DR: VIDRAFT, a Korean AI foundry startup, has open-sourced ViKernel Scanner under Apache 2.0 — a diagnostic tool that tests whether an AI model can be manipulated into making dangerous tool calls, and returns a letter-grade result in under one minute.
